fha.fcDesc: Erroneous air data and inertial reference
fha.phases: Takeoff, Climb, Cruise, Descent, Approach, Landing
fha.effAc: Erroneous air data/inertial reference presents misleading airspeed, altitude or attitude; with three reference units a single erroneous source is outvoted or detectable by comparison, but an undetected erroneous reference feeding displays and flight control drives a large reduction in safety margins that can progress toward loss of control.
fha.effCrew: Physical distress or excessive workload identifying and rejecting the erroneous source; if the error is not detected the crew act on misleading data.
fha.effPax: No occupants in the hold; consequence follows the aircraft outcome.
fha.judgementNote: Turns on whether the three-reference architecture detects/outvotes an erroneous source before it misleads the crew or the flight control law; a robust voting/comparison scheme holds this at Hazardous, while an undetected common erroneous source across sources approaches Catastrophic. The FCS consumes air data/inertial data via the avionics (§5.3.4), so erroneous reference has a flight-control path. Confirm the detection/voting credit at aircraft level.

fha.fcDesc: Undetected erroneous air data and inertial reference
fha.effAc: Erroneous air data and/or inertial reference is presented as valid; primary flight and navigation display drives to erroneous attitude, airspeed or altitude, giving a large reduction in safety margins if the crew acts on it. The independent standby instrument (shares no supply, sensor or processing) remains available as a cross-check but the error is not self-annunciated.
fha.effCrew: Excessive workload to detect the source disagreement and revert to the standby before an unsafe flight state develops; without reliable annunciation the flightcrew cannot be relied upon to detect and act in time in all phases.
fha.effPax: No occupants in the hold; crew only aboard. Physical distress possible if an unsafe flight state develops before reversion.
fha.judgementNote: Turns on whether a comparator/annunciation reliably flags the undetected ADIRU disagreement to the crew in time; the SDD gives three reference units and an independent standby but does not state comparator/voting coverage that self-detects a single erroneous unit. If a validated cross-comparison alerts the crew, this could reduce toward Major; if two units can agree erroneously with no alert, Catastrophic is possible. Confirm with the AVI comparator design and crew-detection HF analysis.

fha.fcDesc: Complete loss of standby flight information
fha.effAc: Loss of the independent standby attitude, airspeed and altitude source; the primary flight and navigation display (three display processors, three reference units) remains fully available, so no reduction in current capability, but the independent backup layer against a subsequent primary failure is lost — a significant reduction in functional capabilities.
fha.effCrew: Significant increase in flightcrew workload to monitor and manage without the standby fallback and to consider dispatch/diversion implications.
fha.effPax: No occupants in the hold; crew only. No physical effect while primaries function normally.
fha.comments: ⚠ PHASES DROPPED — the model named takeoff, climb, cruise, descent, approach, landing, not in this project's phase table; exposure is computed without them. | AI-drafted (claude-opus-4-8). Severity rationale: Major - "significant reduction in safety margins or functional capabilities", AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.3. Standby is the backup layer; with the full primary display and reference set available (§5.11.3) its loss removes redundancy but does not reduce current capability. [anchor MAJ-1 — Major] Levels: Aircraft significant · Crew significant · Occupants none or slight inconvenience → Major (aircraft and crew axes govern). — engineer to confirm.

fha.fcDesc: Partial loss of standby flight information
fha.effAc: Loss of one or more standby parameters (attitude, airspeed or altitude) while primaries remain fully available; a slight-to-significant reduction in the independence of the backup layer, no reduction in current displayed capability.
fha.effCrew: Slight increase in flightcrew workload to note the degraded standby and account for it in contingency planning.
fha.effPax: No occupants in the hold; crew only. No physical effect.
fha.judgementNote: How many standby parameters are lost is not specified; loss of a single parameter with primaries intact could be Minor. Assumed a degraded standby still constitutes a significant loss of the independent backup layer, hence Major; confirm the standby architecture (single integrated unit per §5.11.2 implies partial degradation is unlikely without total loss).

fha.effAc: The standby source presents erroneous attitude, airspeed or altitude while the primary display and its three reference units remain available; the primary set provides the majority reference so an unsafe state is avoided, but the crew's independent fallback is now misleading — a significant reduction in functional capability of the backup layer.
fha.effCrew: Significant increase in flightcrew workload to identify that the standby, not the primaries, is in error and to disregard it; potential for confusion during a concurrent primary anomaly.
fha.effPax: No occupants in the hold; crew only. No physical effect while primaries function.
fha.judgementNote: Assumes the crew resolves the standby-vs-primary disagreement in favour of the primaries; that resolution is reasonable given the primaries carry three reference units against a single standby, but a validated HF/annunciation basis is not stated. If an erroneous standby could be trusted during a concurrent primary degradation, severity rises. Confirm with the AVI source-selection and alerting design.

fha.effAc: Total loss of the consolidated crew alert list means system failures and their procedures are no longer annunciated or prioritised to the crew; subsequent failures may go undetected and unmanaged, giving a large reduction in the crew's ability to cope with adverse operating conditions. Loss of annunciation is itself a failure condition (§5.4.2).
fha.effCrew: Excessive workload to monitor all system states manually without prioritised alerting; the flightcrew cannot be relied upon to detect and act on subsequent failures accurately or completely across all phases.
fha.effPax: No occupants in the hold; crew only. Physical distress possible if an unmanaged subsequent failure develops.
fha.judgementNote: Alerting is driven by two independent processing channels (§5.11.2), so complete loss requires both channels lost; whether residual dedicated warnings (e.g. fire handles, standby annunciators) remain to bound the effect is not fully stated. Assumed the consolidated alert list is the primary detection means whose total loss is Hazardous per §5.4.2 combination logic; confirm residual independent warning coverage and the un-annunciated combination objective.

fha.phases: Taxi, Takeoff, Climb, Cruise, Descent, Approach, Landing
fha.effAc: Some alerts of the consolidated crew-alert list are unavailable; the aircraft continues to fly but a subset of failure conditions would go un-annunciated, giving a significant reduction in functional capabilities to detect and respond to failures.
fha.effCrew: Crew retain the remainder of the alert list plus direct system indications; a significant increase in workload to cross-check system state manually for the affected alerts.
fha.effPax: No effect (hold unoccupied; flight crew only).
fha.judgementNote: Assumed partial loss removes a bounded subset of alerts while the remaining list and direct indications stay available; if a partial loss can silence a catastrophic-linked alert whose detection has no independent means, the class rises. The alert catalogue and its coupling to failure conditions would confirm or overturn this.

Severity rationale: Loss of annunciation is a failure condition in itself, "classified as major unless the applicant can show otherwise" (AC 25.1309-1B §5.4.2); effects match "significant reduction in safety margins or functional capabilities" (AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.3). fha.phases: Taxi, Takeoff, Climb, Cruise, Descent, Approach, Landing
fha.effAc: The alert list presents incorrect status — a real condition mis-prioritised or a wrong alert/procedure shown; crew may act on a false picture, producing a significant reduction in functional capabilities to manage the aircraft correctly.
fha.effCrew: Crew are aware alerting can be erroneous and can cross-check against direct system indications; a significant increase in workload to resolve the discrepancy before acting.
fha.effPax: No effect (hold unoccupied; flight crew only).
fha.judgementNote: Assumed the erroneous alert is detectable by cross-check against independent system indications and the wrong procedure is not itself hazardous to execute. If an erroneous alert could drive a crew action that is catastrophic (e.g. false engine-fire prompting shutdown of a good engine near V1) with no independent cue, the class rises to Hazardous. The alert-to-procedure mapping would settle this.

fha.phases: Taxi, Takeoff, Climb, Cruise, Descent, Approach, Landing
fha.effAc: A spurious alert appears for a condition that has not occurred; no real aircraft capability is lost, but crew attention is diverted.
fha.effCrew: Crew must recognise the alert as spurious by cross-checking system state; a significant increase in workload, greatest if it occurs during a high-workload phase and the crew initiate an unnecessary procedure before dismissing it.
fha.effPax: No effect (hold unoccupied; flight crew only).
fha.judgementNote: Assumed a spurious alert does not by itself command any automatic aircraft response and remains crew-recognisable. If the alert catalogue includes a spurious alert whose associated procedure, if erroneously actioned, degrades a critical function (e.g. spurious fire alert leading to engine shutdown), the class rises. The alert catalogue and any auto-response linkage would confirm this.

fha.fcDesc: Undetected partial loss of crew alerting
fha.phases: Taxi, Takeoff, Climb, Cruise, Descent, Approach, Landing
fha.effAc: A subset of alerts is silently unavailable and the loss itself is not annunciated; failure conditions in the affected subset would occur with no alert and no crew awareness that alerting is degraded, giving a large reduction in functional capabilities to detect failures.
fha.effCrew: Crew continue normal duties unaware that part of the alert list is inoperative; they receive no cue to cross-check the affected functions and may not detect the underlying condition until its effect is felt.
fha.effPax: No effect (hold unoccupied; flight crew only).
fha.judgementNote: Assumed the undetected subset can include alerts for conditions whose only credited detection is the alert list, so silence leaves the crew with no cue. If every function in the affected subset retains an independent direct indication the crew habitually monitor, the class falls to Major. The alerting architecture's dual-channel monitoring coverage (§5.11.2, two independent channels) and the alert-to-function map would settle this.

[anchor HAZ-1 — Hazardous] Levels: Aircraft large · Crew significant · Occupants none or slight inconvenience → Hazardous (aircraft axis governs). — engineer to confirm.

fha.phases: Taxi, Takeoff, Climb, Cruise, Descent, Approach, Landing
fha.effAc: The alert list presents incorrect status and the error is not detectable by the crew; crew act on a false picture — actioning a procedure for a non-existent condition, or not actioning a real one — giving a large reduction in functional capabilities to manage the aircraft correctly.
fha.effCrew: Crew take the erroneous alert at face value with no cue to cross-check; they may execute an inappropriate procedure or omit a required one, without recognising the alerting is wrong.
fha.effPax: No effect (hold unoccupied; flight crew only).
fha.judgementNote: Assumed an undetected erroneous alert can misdirect crew into or out of a safety-critical action but not directly command a catastrophic outcome without any subsequent cue. If the mapped procedure for a plausible erroneous alert is itself catastrophic to execute with no recovery cue, the class rises to Catastrophic. The alert-to-procedure map and the dual-channel comparison monitoring (§5.11.2) would confirm or overturn this.
